segments.text: Sometimes it may be necessary for us to tell our Indian exporters, sorry guys, we have to risk American sanctions and you may lose your market there, but we have made it easy for you to find markets elsewhere else in the world.
We have signed FTAs with so many countries, the EU, the UK, Australia, Oman, New Zealand, whatever, you can go off and try and sell goods to other markets.
But I'm afraid we cannot save you from America because we cannot afford to lose our imports from Russia.
China will not necessarily be a big obstacle when it comes to something like coming up with a joint declaration.
The problem will be the disagreement between Iran and UAE.
UAE feels that Iran has been unfairly hitting it with missiles.
Iran feels that the UAE and other Gulf countries have provided a base to America to hit them.
And that kind of divergence may not be easy to reconcile in a joint declaration.
The Prime Minister will have an opportunity to have really great conversations with countries that to some degree we have been neglecting of late.
It's been a long time since we've had a serious bilateral with Egypt, which is an important relationship for us, with South Africa.
We have a number of interesting issues and of course the whole African relationship is important.
The Africa Forum Summit has been delayed yet again this year.
It should have happened a few years ago and we are running late on this.
Maybe talking to South Africa and Ethiopia about our engagement with Africa will equally be important.
So beyond the headlines.
Sir, you know BRICS has been expanded.
If I may ask you, because there is a lot of debate who the real friend of India is.
Which country could India trust the most among all the countries which are coming to participate?
Of course, we recognize him as Prime Minister of Bangladesh.
And I'm very puzzled by the statement by the official sources in Dhaka.
It truly surprises me.
I don't think there was any doubt in extending the invitation that we were honoring the Prime Minister of Bangladesh, who happens also to be Chairman of IMSTEK and is an observer of BRICS.
We have been historically of the view that BRICS is non-West, but not anti-West.
That's not always the use to which some of its members have tried to put it.
They have tried to turn it in an anti-West direction.
And India has no interest in that.
We are not keen on becoming seen as a member of an anti-Western geopolitical grouping.
So the geopolitics of BRICS have always been for us something we're much more cautious about, as opposed to issues of economics, of trade, of development cooperation, of global governance, and so on.
Those are the areas where we saw BRICS as a natural platform.
Sir, you use the word tangible.
Interestingly, your fellow MP, Congress MP, Mr. P. Chidambaram also used this word and he said that he has not seen any tangible outcomes of previous BRICS summits.
BRICS was established in 2009, is the new development bank, which happened when he was finance minister.
There's been nothing else since then.
I have, perhaps because of my years of international service, I have a slightly broader view of the value of such forums.
They cannot only be measured in terms of tangible outcomes.
He is totally correct that there are no concrete, tangible outcomes.
What can we point to that came out of this?
I think India should veto Pakistani entry simply because we have absolutely nothing to gain from it.

Pakistan gains a platform without having in any way reformed its intransigent behavior towards us, without having taken any steps to dismantle the infrastructure of terrorism on their soil that has been harming us.
Why should we give them a concession?
India is hosting 18th summit of BRICS.
Everyone is asking, what would India achieve?
Hello, viewers.
I'm your host, Neeta Sharma.
Welcome to Indian Express.
In conversation today, we have Shashi Tharoor, Congress MP, who is also chairman of Standing Committee on Ministry of External Affairs.
We will try to understand from him as to what all deliverables is India eyeing on.
So thank you so much for speaking to Indian Express.
Good evening.
First thing that now the China has agreed that the Chinese premier is coming to India, there is going to be a bilateral and obviously the bilateral is going to remain in the headlines.
So what do you expect from the bilateral and can India cooperate with China in BRICS while the LSE issue still is not resolved?
No, look, I think India is very wisely continuing its cooperation with China or with any other country in the BRICS platform and in other global or multilateral platforms.
We remain a key member, after all, of BRICS.
And so BRICS as a platform is important in its own right.
It demonstrates India's convening power and global influence, and that's all very good for us.
But at the same time, it gives us an opportunity to have bilateral meetings with visiting heads of state and government.
of which China is one, and arguably, as you said, the one that may get the most attention, though I think our bilateral with President Putin will also get a lot of media attention around the world.
But there'll also be other meetings with, frankly, heads of state and government of BRICS, but also some of the observer countries which are coming at the highest levels.
so that the Prime Minister will have an opportunity to have really great conversations with countries that to some degree we have been neglecting of late.
It's been a long time since we've had a serious bilateral with Egypt, which is an important relationship for us with South Africa.
where we have a number of interesting issues and of course the whole African relationship is important.
The India Africa Forum Summit has been delayed yet again this year.
It should have happened a few years ago and we are running late on this.
Maybe talking to South Africa and Ethiopia about our engagement with Africa.
will equally be important.
So beyond the headlines, each of these bilateral meetings has a value in promoting our national interest.

Now, as far as meeting the Chinese is concerned, which is your specific question, I would say there is no doubt in my mind that this is an important relationship and it has not been a happy relationship for the last half a dozen years.
One could argue that the onus is on China because Galwan was a completely unprovoked transgression by them, which resulted in the deaths of 20 Javans.
And we will clearly want to restore the status quo ante, which is not, strictly speaking, fully happened.
The patrols have been resumed and so on, but we're not quite where we were as of, you know, May 2020.
Then you have to look at things like the continued Chinese assertiveness.
First of all, on the border where they've been probing our border in many places and clearly taking steps to alter the realities on the ground in ways that are inimical to India's interests.
Secondly, their weaponization of trade by withholding things like the rare earths, tunnel boring machines, power substations, all sorts of essential ingredients and elements for Indian manufacturers.
We have allowed ourselves to become dependent on China and China has used that, weaponized it to say, look buddies, we have leverage over you that you don't have over us.
And each time they withhold something, it's a lesson to India that India should better oblige the Chinese or they will kick us around.
But that's not something that any self-respecting country is going to tolerate.
And India has every interest in using this platform to say, look, if you make a friendly gesture to us, we're ready to reciprocate.
We don't want trouble on our borders.
We want to focus on the development of our own nation and the well-being of our own people.
But if you're going to be playing hardball with us, we know how to play hardball back.
It may not be the same way, but we will also understand what to do.
So I think the important challenge in these bilateral meetings is,
Don't confuse them with your relationship in BRICS, which is a multilateral relationship.

Take the bilateral relationship on its own terms and conduct your conversations with an eye fundamentally on your own national interest only, not the interests of BRICS or any other collective grouping, just your national interest.
And that's how the bilateral should run.
Bricks, on the other hand, we may find common ground with China on a lot of issues and bricks.
In fact, China will not necessarily be a big obstacle when it comes to something like coming up with a joint declaration.
The problem will be the disagreement between Iran and UAE.
UAE feels that Iran has been unfairly hitting it with missiles.
Iran feels that the UAE and other Gulf countries have provided a base to America to hit them.
And that kind of divergence may not be easy to reconcile in a joint declaration.
People point out that the Shanghai Cooperation Organization was able to have a joint declaration, but they forget that UAE is not a member of that.
So in this forum, there are particular challenges that will exercise India's chairmanship and challenge the skills of our diplomacy.
But always remember that the important consideration for us has to remain our national interest.
So if, for example, Russia and Iran press this alternative BRICS currency idea, de-dollarization, I think India will want to resist that.
Why would we want to give up the dollar to be in a new currency that is dominated by the Chinese yuan?
We'll have to really have some serious discussions on all this.
What we are more interested in is local currency trade.
Where we buy goods from Russia and pay rupees and they sell us goods and we pay rubles or vice versa, rupees from our side, rubles from them.
This is the kind of stuff that, to be very honest, no country can object to.
Why would Washington object for any sovereign nation to use its own currency for any purpose that may be deemed legal?
As far as I'm concerned, that's the kind of thing that we could still do.
But when it comes to a collective decision, be very wary because at the moment, China has not given us enough reason to believe that they have our best interests at heart.
Absolutely.
So as you mentioned, the next big country is Russia and Modi put in meetings are also happening.
Interestingly, Russia wants energy and sanctions relief, while India wants cheap oil without becoming sanctions target.
Where should New Delhi draw a red line as far as Delhi is concerned?
Look, this is a very tough call, because we don't really know Washington's intentions.
The Senate passed a law which President Trump has signed, which authorizes him to levy 100% sanctions on us if we continue buying Russian oil.
Now, let's be very blunt and say 100% sanctions means any Indian item with that level of sanctions that becomes unviable in the American market is simply not feasible to sell it anymore.
in which case you're talking about something so fundamental that India has to take a call that's compatible with its self-respect and its needs.
Either we do what we did with Iran when Iran was sanctioned, and we dramatically cut back on our oil imports, gas imports from Iran, and we even cut back on our involvement in the Shah Baha project.
Out of respect for American sanctions, we felt that honoring those sanctions was more important to us than preserving trade with Iran.
We may not have the same calculation when it comes to Russia, because Russia, after all, is a country with whom the scale is enormous.
And our dependence on imports of energy, for example, is so colossal that if we can't buy Russian oil, we may be paying much more money to get oil from any other country.
from farther away, like Venezuela or Guyana can sell us oil, but the transport costs are going to be dramatically greater than from Russia.
So all of these things India will have to think about.
And I cannot substitute myself for the government's judgment because the government has access to information, numbers and facts that I don't have and you don't have.
So we will have to see.
But I'm hoping the government will weigh all this into account in deciding how to proceed on something like that.

Sometimes it may be necessary for us to tell our Indian exporters, sorry guys, we have to risk American sanctions and you may lose your market there, but we have made it easy for you to find markets elsewhere else in the world.
We have signed FTAs with so many countries, the EU, the UK, Australia, Oman, New Zealand, whatever, you can go off and try and sell goods to other markets.
But I'm afraid we cannot save you from America because we cannot afford to lose our imports from Russia.
That kind of calculation.
On the other hand, maybe we can persuade Washington to continue giving us time and breathing space to work on continuing this relationship.
But bluntly speaking, that calculation only the government can make and they will have to make it because acquiescing in American sanctions is potentially hugely problematic.
we are not only buying crude oil from Russia, but we are selling refined oil products, petrol products to Russia too.
Now that's both ways trade.
Russia is also an export market for us and given that our import dependencies have gone up so much, we need to keep cultivating our export markets.
You have to understand that we are
an extraordinarily important grouping BRICS.
The majority of the world's population is in BRICS, and 41% of global GDP is accounted for by the BRICS countries.
It's not a small group.
It's not a minor thing.
So we'll have to take all these pluses and minuses into account.
In fact, one of the concerns generally with trade with the BRICS countries is that intra-BRICS trade has been growing, but not in our favor.
Our exports to BRICS countries are going down and our imports from BRICS countries are going up.
So we need to use the BRICS platform to see how we can try and restore a little bit of balance there and get more of our goods exported to BRICS countries.

So interestingly, another headline which is coming, Bangladesh Prime Minister Mr. Tariq Rehman is not attending BRICS summit because his foreign minister claims that he was not invited in the capacity of the prime minister.
So what does it say about relations between India and Bangladesh, if I may ask you?

It says that there is certainly some great confusion about vocabulary because we certainly can only invite Tariq Rehman as prime minister because as a head of government of an observer country, he would be most welcome.
The fact is that he's also the chairman of BIMSTEC.
So it may be what they're saying is that we invited him as chairman of BIMSTEC, we didn't invite him as prime minister of Bangladesh.
But why is he chairman of BIMSTEC?
Because he's prime minister of Bangladesh.
So that seems to me a clutching at straws kind of argument.
Of course, we recognize him as prime minister of Bangladesh.
And I'm very puzzled by the statement by the official sources in Dhaka.
It truly surprises me.
I don't think there was any doubt in extending the invitation that we were honoring the prime minister of Bangladesh, who happens also to be chairman of IMSTEK and is an observer of BRICS.
I mean, that is a tripartite, shall we say,
set of titles, it's not a withdrawal of any title.
I find that very odd indeed.
In fact, his foreign minister came out and gave a statement.
Moving to the next question, sir, Iran and UAE will also sit in the same groupings in BRIC.
Can India produce a joint declaration on West Asia even though the conflict continues there, though the foreign minister's level talk also did not get any joint declaration then also?
Correct.
When the foreign ministers met in the summer, we could not agree a joint declaration.
And to be very honest, it's exactly the same issue.
It is the fact that both sides feel that they are unfairly being victimized and targeted.
Iran feels that the Gulf countries have provided basis for the Americans to attack them.
And the Gulf countries feel that Iran is unfairly attacking them for foreign policy decisions by America that they have nothing to do with.
So both ways there is a strong perception of unfairness, but today the UAE is not even talking bilaterally to Iran.
So when they meet on the common table inside the common room of the BRICS, I don't even know if they will say hello to each other, acknowledge each other's presence.
So in those circumstances, to predict that we can find an agreed formula, to my mind looks tough.
If we do pull something off, then that would be a great triumph of Indian diplomacy.
But I can tell you that
While people are saying, well, look, the SCO was able to find a formula acceptable to everyone.
They are forgetting that in the SCO, there is no UAE.
So the fact is we would really have a different kind of challenge.
The backup option of a chairman's declaration by India laying out the discussions might still be a viable possibility.
And we will have to see, honestly, if that is the best we can come up with.
But let's not judge the BRICS platform only by such issues.
Yes, there are divergences, but the very fact that despite these divergences, we're going to get everyone around the table is no mean accomplishment.
It demonstrates India's convening power.
It demonstrates our global influence in the world.
And I think all of us would value the importance of that.
So as you mentioned that Intra Bricks trade is still very China heavy.
So how will India stop Bricks from becoming a market for Chinese goods rather than the voice of Global South?
Well, it's all of these things.
I mean, don't forget, Brick started off invented by an economist from the Goldman Sachs Bank who saw it as a platform of emerging markets.
From that modest beginning, we have our ambitions and our role has grown.
So we've done certainly we've spoken for the emerging markets collectively.
We have tried to promote economic cooperation between us and we have created the new development bank, which has been of tangible benefit to India because we are
joint sort of contributors to it as is China, but we are also big recipients from it, which is very important for us to get from the new development bank.
So that's been a positive, tangible outcome.

But then beyond that, we have used BRICS as a platform to advance our interests and global governance issues in things like permanent representation of the Global South and multilateral forums, reforming the World Bank and the IMF's voting rights, talking about the
the Security Council reform, all sorts of areas where global agendas have also been pursued by us through BRICS.
So I would not write off the value of all of these things.

I personally would concede, and I have written myself, that BRICS has by and large, with the exception of the creation of the New Development Bank, it's by and large been longer on lofty sentiment and grand declarations and rhetoric than it has been on tangible outcomes.
But that's often a failure of large multinational groupings.
It doesn't matter because actually getting people around a table has value in itself.
And I would like to say that that value is something we should certainly use.
And I think one important thing about our chairmanship this year, don't forget that next year China is the chairman.
So we should lay down some very clear lines coming out of the summit.
that will perhaps limit or draw lines around how far the grouping can go under some other chairman like China, which may have a very different agenda.
We have been historically of the view that BRICS is non-West, but not anti-West.
That's not always the use to which some of its members have tried to put it.
They have tried to turn it in an anti-West direction.
And India has no interest in that.
We are not keen on becoming seen as a member of an anti-Western geopolitical grouping.
So the geopolitics are bricks.
have always been for us something we're much more cautious about, as opposed to issues of economics, of trade, of development cooperation, of global governance and so on.
Those are the areas where we saw BRICS as a natural platform and less so on global geopolitics, but inevitably geopolitics comes.
I'm not saying we can avoid it.
I'm just saying that we should understand that judging BRICS principally by something that is not much more than an afterthought is not entirely wise.
So you use the word tangible.
Interestingly, your fellow MP, Congress MP, Mr. P Chidambaram also used this word.
And he said that he has not seen any tangible outcomes of previous BRIC summits.
Your take.

No, he's right about that in the sense that if you're judging it by concrete outcomes, the only thing you can point to since BRICS was established in 2009 is the new development bank, which happened when he was finance minister.
There's been nothing else since then.
I have, perhaps because of my years of international service, I have a slightly broader view of the value of such forums.
They cannot only be measured in terms of tangible outcomes.
He is totally correct that there are no concrete tangible outcomes.
What can we point to that came out of this?
But the intangible outcomes also have value.

And the intangible outcomes are in terms of global influence, convening power, demonstrating networking capacity, and an excuse to conduct important bilateral conversations that might not otherwise have taken place, certainly not in one venue at one time very easily.
I mean, what Mr. Modi would have needed 15 different bilateral visits to meet these 15 presidents, he can do in the comfort of his own capital over two days.
That's not a small matter.
That's a tangible thing if you want.
But even if you think of it as intangible, it's not bad.
So, you know, BRICS has been expanded.
If I may ask you, because there is a lot of debate, who the real friend of India is, which country could India trust the most among all the countries which are coming to participate?
Look, most of them have been very friendly with us.
I think to be very honest, we've only had severely tense relationships with China out of the 11 members because Russia has been friendly and important source of both oil and defense parts.
UAE is very close to us in the Gulf.
We have very close understanding.
Egypt is an important partner going back to the non-line days and remains a close friend of ours on the global stage.
Ethiopia has been a friendly relationship.
There are no tensions dividing us.
South Africa has been a major associate of ours on the UN and other places, etc.
Go on down the list.
You don't really have any enemies or negatives of India.
And I think we should actually be very happy to see the fact that so many friends are on the table.
That doesn't mean we agree with them on everything.
You have to understand that there is a situation where each country will have a different nuance, a different emphasis, a different way of seeing certain problems.
South Africa may be far more condemnatory of Israel than we are.
For example, some of the Arab countries in the

in the BRICS grouping are those that have not been at all hostile to us, even on issues like Kashmir, but they may have a position on some issues in the West Asian security ambit, which may not be exactly as nuanced as we would like it to be, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.
There are a lot of things in any multilateral grouping where you have to draw a clear distinction between what is multilateral and what is bilateral.
Multilaterally, you can make common cause with a lot of countries with whom bilaterally you may want to nuance things a little better.
Last two questions, China and Russia have also been open to Pakistan's entry in BRICS.
In your view, should India veto any such move?
I think India should veto Pakistani entry simply because we have absolutely nothing to gain from it.

Pakistan gains a platform without having in any way reformed its intransigent behavior towards us, without having taken any steps to dismantle the infrastructure of terrorism on their soil that has been harming us.
Why should we give them a concession?
In fact, as you know, when Pakistani terrorists come to India and we try and sanction them at the UN Security Council, China is the one that protects China, Pakistan repeatedly over and over again.
I think on these things, you know, we have to show that two can play the same game.
We are not going to be the kind of bad seas who will
simply lie over and be obliging to everyone all the time.
I think it's important that we remember our national interests and our self-respect in any of these issues.
Frankly, we were very skeptical about expansion to begin with.
Even before the expansion from 5 to 11, we were very skeptical.
And we insisted in the declaration at that time that we must have an expansion only on the basis of full consultation and consensus.
That and consensus means that we have a veto, as is anybody else on any expansion.
And we will make sure that if there are some people coming on board we're not totally comfortable with, that others will come on board we're more comfortable with.
That's the way in which we'll make sure that any expansion that happens is not inimical to our interests.
Sir, but as far as the SEO is concerned, now Pakistan is going to take over SEO presidency.
So how significant is this for India?
SEO has always been seen by the whole world as a China dominated, China led grouping with even a Chinese city in the name of the organization.
Russia has made common cause with China and a lot of these things.
Some of the other members have been very happy to attach themselves to the coattails of these two.
Pakistan, as you know, in many ways is a wholly owned subsidiary of China.
So we're not going to suddenly discover sort of new qualities in SCO that we had not suspected existed.
These are all there.
We're very aware of it.
I think it's part of India's strategic autonomy and its multi-alignment policy that we will keep links with everybody, even forums in which we are not as happy or in which we are not as welcome even.

But we will do it because, you know, it's better to be there, keeping our eyes and ears open and ensuring that nothing happens that is fundamentally hostile to our interests, which we've been able to do in this year.
They've never sort of adopted any declaration directly hostile to us.
So if Pakistan tries to get up to any mischief, there are other members who we can ask very bluntly, do you want Pakistan as chair to really destroy the viability of this organization?
Do you want us to walk out?
Or are you prepared to persuade your Pakistani friends that keeping India on board is a value for the SEO and therefore that you should actually work with us to accommodate our concerns?
I believe the latter will prevail.
I don't see why China or Russia.
should give Pakistan a free run as chair to do things that India will be offended by.
And I don't think, if anything, I think this Pakistani chairmanship could become an opportunity for Pakistan to demonstrate some sort of decency and good faith towards us.
They've been feeling for some time that this complete absence of dialogue is only hurting them.
And I think if they want to create through SCO,
a sort of a situation where they can talk to us, either on the margins of SEO or on the forum itself.
I think they would be unwise to try and do anything hostile to us through their chairmanship.
So as the chairman of the Standing Committee of Parliament and Ministry of External Affairs, what is the biggest headlines that you would hope that this BRICS summit would bring out?
Well, look, I mean, the biggest headline would certainly be an agreed declaration on all issues, but I'm not expecting that.
I think that would be a near miracle.
And if we pull that off, it's a great triumph for Indian diplomacy.
Short of that, what would I expect?
Good atmospherics, excellent bilaterals on the margins where the prime minister meets world leaders from various countries we want to strengthen our relationships with.
And at the same time, perhaps the fact that
the BRICS is happening at all, enhances Delhi's stature on the global stage.
As an Indian, that's something that I would like to see, that we are once again regarded as a significant player.
Imagine if this BRICS summit had taken place with only one or two presidents coming.
It would not have been seen, it would have been seen as a damp squib.
Instead you've got a huge event with more than a dozen heads of state and government ministers, counting the ones from observer countries who are coming at that level.
And I think this could be an extraordinary advertisement for us if we host it right and well.
It's going to be an absolute traffic nightmare and security nightmare.

I'll be observing it from the US, but I can say that as far as as far as I'm concerned, this is something that we could all end up patting ourselves in the back about, or we could end up with egg on our faces.
I just don't want the headline to be the latter.
I want it to be the former.
Beyond that, details we don't know.
Let's wait till the 13th or 14th to see what comes out of the meeting.
Thank you so much for sharing such valuable insights and you have a safe trip and enjoy yourself wherever you are right now.
Thank you so much.
Thank you.
Now, I came to collect an award from the Foreign Policy Association.
Their prestigious medal was given to me.
It's a Medal of Honor.
So that was the main reason I was here.
And since I wasn't invited to anything to do with the BRICS, I thought I would rather come and collect this prestigious medal.
So here I am.
Thank you very much.
Thank you, sir.
Thank you.
Take care.
